title: The Delicate Task of Assigning a Team Member’s Idea to Someone Else
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article tackles a sensitive leadership moment: reassigning execution of an idea away from the team member who originated it, because they lack the skills to bring it to fruition. The piece distinguishes origination from execution as two separate skills and offers a script for the reassignment conversation — leading with genuine praise, framing the decision around project fit rather than personal shortcomings, avoiding phrases like "you're not ready," and offering an elevated role like advisor or consultant to preserve dignity. It stresses ensuring the originator still receives visible credit throughout execution, and frames the goal as leaving them disappointed but not discouraged, since ultimately the team's success matters more than any one person's ownership.
points: Origination and execution of an idea are two distinct skills — not everyone excels at both.
The reassignment conversation should open with genuine praise and frame the decision around project needs, not personal shortcomings.
Offering an elevated role (advisor, reviewer, consulting director) helps preserve the originator's dignity and continued involvement.
Ensuring visible credit throughout execution helps the originator remain disappointed but not discouraged.
quotes: in many cases, they lack the skills, experience, or talent to execute on their own idea.
Ideas have two distinct stages—origination and execution. Not everyone is good at both.
The feedback should begin with genuine praise for the idea and their role in producing it.
it is best to frame the decision around role fit and project needs rather than on personal shortcomings.
The outcome leaders hope for is for the originator to be mildly disappointed but not discouraged.
